items.title: Jack Teagarden Interview, 1959-10-29
items.q: Ray Baduke, who's a New Orleans boy here, was, we got him on drums so Benny could, uh, uh, stand in front with a baton.

ctx.x: Okay, whenever you're ready. Well, how did you learn trombone and develop your style? That's what I really like to know.

Well, I'll tell you, when I was, uh, pretty young, my mother and I used to play in, uh, the old silent movie theaters. We used to play for the comedies and, uh, I don't know, just trombone and piano. You know, learn more technique because I had the whole, swing the whole thing, melody and all. You know. And, uh, my mother played very good ragtime piano, which was very good for those years. Then, uh, I lost my father in 1918 with the flu. And then I went, we went to Oklahoma City. And I went one more year of, uh,…

Can we back up for a minute and go back to your early period? Yeah. Because there's some particular people I'd like to ask you about some particular things. What kind of training did Peg Kelly have that he should develop this wonderful style?

items.title: Ray Bauduc Interview, 1984-06-27
items.q: And Jack Teagarden was on trombone, see.

ctx.x: So you, well, you'd come back for a visit though, on vacation or something.

I came back, I came back in 1940. No, I didn't, I didn't get back until 1940. I think I, I, I, I went to, I think it was my dad's funeral or my mother's. I can't remember which one, 1940. Because I was in the Army when, when the other, one of the, one of the other died and I was out of Vallejo, California at that time. But anyway, but the, the only time I, I got home, I, I, I got home on a vacation when I was with Ben Pollack's band. I don't remember now. We were playing at the Florentine Grill Room at the Park…

Yeah, I, I, I thought maybe you'd come back when you were pretty rich. I read something about a show that Charles Dillingham had. Do you know that name? Dillingham. Yeah, Charles Dillingham had a show. Where? In New York. This was in the, this was in the, in the local, you know, uh, 174 magazine. The Union magazine, yeah.

items.title: Jack Teagarden Interview, 1959-10-30
items.q: I got him a job with Benny Pollack

ctx.x: You see, as soon as he gets his time, he will. Yeah. Picture. Say Jack, how did Ray Perdue get his first break? I've heard this story before. I wanted to get that down. I didn't ask that last night.
Well, the first time I met him, he was, he went on sort of a cross country, Barnstorm trip with Charlie, with Johnny Bar's doctor.

items.title: Ray Bauduc and Nappy Lamare Interview, 1959-09-09
items.q: They had Jack Teague on and Jimmy McPartland and Big Braider's on piano.

ctx.x: Can I ask Ray a little bit about when you played with Ben Pollock? Did he just use a stick to the director or what did he do?

Well, he used a stick on a drum, which we got in plenty of arguments about. Well, it was a funny thing. Benny Pollock had the most wonderful band I ever heard in my life. That was including Benny Goodman in the band. They had Jack Teague on and Jimmy McPartland and Big Braider's on piano. I think Dick Morgan was playing banjo and guitar there and Harry Goodman on bass. I think Al Harris played first trumpet. And the saxophone, well, of course, they had Gil Roden and Benny Goodman and Larry Binion, I think, was…
Well, are you watching the time? Yeah. How much? We don't want to take off your whole intermission.
